reason: A perianth can be bell-shaped, and the examples are correct.
A calyx can have silky hairs, and the examples are correct.
The examples (margins, apex) point to a leaf-like part. Fleshy leaves are normal. I did not look up the FLOPO class name, so check it.
An indusium (the cover over a fern sorus) can have an entire margin.
Fruits and pods can be velvety, and the examples are correct.

'Attachment quality' is too general. The examples mean 'has a stalk' (stipitate). A rule would have to map stipitate or stipe wording to a stalk-presence value, or to a stipe part. It should not map to the generic attribute.
Leaf margins can be recurved or plane (flat), and curvature is the right attribute.
A narrow bract is a decreased width, and the examples are correct.
Wrong bearer. The counts are spores per sporangium or capsule, so the count belongs to the sporangium, not to the spore.
A floral disc can be fleshy. Examples like 'with 5 fleshy glands' describe a part of the disc, which is a small flaw.
Corona segments can have a colour, including a colour that changes along the part. I did not look up the FLOPO class name.
A stylopodium (swelling at the style base in Apiaceae) is often conical.
Wrong reading. French 'discolore' means the two leaf faces differ in colour, not that the leaf has lost or changed colour. A rule for 'faces of different colour' is needed.
A corolla or its limb can have an entire margin.
Petals can taper toward the base or apex.
An orchid column can be curved, and the examples are correct.
Veins and veinlets can form a network (reticulate), and the examples are correct.
A floral disc can be cup-shaped.
A corolla margin, claw or ring can have marginal hairs (ciliate).
Wrong bearer. 'Leaves few' is a count of leaves on the plant or shoot, so the leaf is the wrong bearer. A rule should attach it to the whole that carries the leaves.
Inflorescence axes can be scabrid or rough. The generic texture attribute with a value like scabrid is fine.
A petiole can persist or fall off, and the examples are correct.
Fruits and capsules can persist. Some examples (septa, floral remnant) belong to other parts, which is a small flaw.
An interrupted inflorescence is discontinuous, and the examples are correct.

The examples are counts of pedicels per node or per subtending leaf, not a count of one pedicel. A rule must attach the count to the parent that carries the pedicels. 'Present or absent' is a different pattern.
The abaxial leaf epidermis can be papillose. This is a texture value.
A prickle cannot be 'present' as its own quality. Presence or absence belongs to the parent (stem, leaf) through the has-part pattern. The examples are about prickle position or teeth.
A flower bract has a length, and the examples are correct.
The examples are the depth of lobes or teeth ('deep in distal half', 'deeply dentate'). A rule would have to tell lobe or incision depth, which belongs to the margin or lobe, from sepal depth.
A receptacle or receptacular cup can be bell-shaped.
A leaf sheath can fit tightly around the stem.
Leaflets or their segments can spread.
Fruits can be keeled (carinate), and the examples are correct.
Wrong part. The French 'éperon pendant' is a spur (floral spur), not a short shoot. The part mapping is wrong, so fix it in the lexicon rather than allow this pair.
A leaf blade can be ascending.
Margins and apex can be entire. This matches the leaf-like reading of this class.
Presence or absence of the indusium belongs to the parent (frond or pinna). The examples include hairs and 'indusiate', which are mixed readings.
A stigma can be enlarged or large relative to the style.
A staminal column has a length, and the examples are correct.
Flowers can be borne in fascicles. The examples are correct in sense, although the count of flowers per fascicle is also mixed in.
A samara cannot be 'present' as its own quality. Presence belongs to the parent through the has-part pattern. 'Samara wing' and 'Samaracetums' are mixed readings.
Lateral veins can ascend, and the examples are correct.
A moss peristome (teeth ring) has a length, given in µm.
Leaf blades can be folded lengthwise.
A utricle surface can be papillose or scabrous. Some examples are about the beak or wing, which is a small flaw.
An ovary can be scaly (lepidote).
Stems and scapes can be thread-like (filiform).
Domatia cannot be 'present' as their own quality. Presence or absence belongs to the leaf through the has-part pattern. 'Tufts of hairs' describes what the domatia are.

The examples (membranous, fibrous, 'without fibers') are different values of a part wall or covering. I did not look up the class. A rule would need to map membranous and fibrous to their own value terms and not to the generic texture attribute.
A sepal surface can be scaly (lepidote).
Fruit margins can have hairs (ciliate or ciliolate).
Wrong part. The examples say 'spur', which is a floral spur, not a short shoot. The part mapping is wrong, so fix it in the lexicon rather than allow this pair.
The examples are the number of primary veins per leaf, so the count belongs to the leaf or lamina and not to one vein. A rule would need to attach the count to the parent that carries the veins.
A cyathium has a size. The examples give length × width, so the width should be read as well.
An orchid column can be winged.
Achenes can be triangular in outline or cross-section.
Involucral bracts can differ in orientation (erect, spreading, appressed). The generic position attribute with these values is acceptable.
Leaf blade surfaces can be silky.
Leaf or culm sheaths can fall off (deciduous).
Achenes can be glandular, and the examples are correct.
